items.stem: As large corporations grew in the Gilded Age, they employed growing numbers of clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, and stenographers. These white-collar jobs existed mainly because
options: (A) factory owners needed more manual laborers to operate the new machinery
(B) large corporations needed office workers to handle paperwork, accounts, and coordination across their operations
(C) the federal government hired millions of new civil servants under civil service reform, creating a government workforce larger than the private office workforce
(D) immigrants refused to do factory work, so employers created office jobs instead
items.explanation: Corporate growth created the need for office staff: big firms had paperwork, accounts, and far-flung operations to manage, and clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, and stenographers did that non-manual work.

option_explanations.A: These were office jobs, not manual-labor jobs; factory hands operated the machinery.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Expanding corporations needed armies of office workers to manage their paperwork and coordination.
option_explanations.C: Civil service reform affected only a small federal workforce, not millions of workers.
option_explanations.D: Immigrants filled factory jobs in large numbers; office jobs were not created as a substitute for factory labor.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — corporations needed armies of clerks, bookkeepers, managers, salesmen, stenographers

items.stem: The spread of machines like the 1890 typewriter shown here helped change the makeup of the American office workforce because
options: (A) typewriters eliminated the need for office workers entirely
(B) only men were permitted to operate typewriters in American offices
(C) employers hired large numbers of women as typists and stenographers as typewriters and telephones multiplied
(D) typewriters required every manager to write out all correspondence by hand
items.explanation: The typewriter and the telephone created new clerical jobs, and employers filled those jobs — typist, stenographer, telephone operator — largely with women, bringing women into the office workforce in large numbers.

option_explanations.A: Typewriters created office jobs rather than eliminating them.
option_explanations.B: Women, not men alone, became the main operators of these machines in offices.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The new office machines opened clerical work to large numbers of women.
option_explanations.D: Managers dictated or assigned correspondence; the new machines did not return managers to handwriting.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — women entered the office workforce in large numbers as typewriters and telephones multiplied

stimulus.image_caption: Newspaper advertisement for H. Leh & Company department store, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1890.

items.stem: This 1890 newspaper advertisement for a department store illustrates the beginnings of a consumer culture in the Gilded Age. Department stores such as Macy's, Marshall Field's, and Wanamaker's changed American shopping by
options: (A) offering fixed prices, advertised goods, and brand names, and making shopping itself a leisure activity
(B) selling only luxury goods that ordinary middle-class families could not afford, serving a tiny elite of wealthy shoppers
(C) requiring every customer to haggle over the price of each item
(D) conducting all of their business through mail-order catalogs
items.explanation: Department stores built consumer culture on fixed prices, advertising, and brand names, and they made shopping a leisure pastime — the ad itself, listing goods with set prices, is an example of the new advertising.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Fixed prices, advertising, brand names, and shopping as leisure were the department store's innovations.
option_explanations.B: Department stores served the broad middle class, not only the wealthy.
option_explanations.C: Fixed prices replaced haggling; that was one of the stores' defining changes.
option_explanations.D: Mail-order catalogs were the business of Montgomery Ward and Sears, not of the big city department stores.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's); fixed prices, advertising, brand names, shopping as leisure

stimulus.image_caption: Floor plan of the first floor of Macy's Department Store, New York, as built 1901–1902.

items.stem: The image is the 1902 floor plan of the first floor of Macy's department store in New York. As a piece of historical evidence, this plan best supports which conclusion?
options: (A) Most Americans did their shopping in department stores by 1902
(B) department stores caused the decline of small-town general stores, since every rural family abandoned local shops to travel to the city
(C) Macy's sold a larger volume of goods than any other American retailer
(D) department stores were large, carefully organized retail enterprises built to display a wide variety of goods under one roof
items.explanation: The plan shows a single floor divided into many departments for different goods — direct evidence of the department store's scale and deliberate organization. It says nothing about national shopping habits, causes of other stores' decline, or sales rankings.

option_explanations.A: One store's floor plan cannot show where most Americans shopped.
option_explanations.B: The plan shows one building's layout; it cannot establish what caused another kind of store to decline.
option_explanations.C: A floor plan shows layout, not sales volume or rank among retailers.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The plan documents a large retail space deliberately divided into departments for displaying many kinds of goods.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — department stores (Macy's, Marshall Field's, Wanamaker's); beginnings of consumer culture

stimulus.image_caption: Stereoscopic view of the Montgomery Ward & Co. establishment, Chicago.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 19th-century stereoscopic view, Robert N. Dennis collection; LicenseShortName Public domain

items.stem: The stereoscopic view shows the Montgomery Ward & Co. building in Chicago. Firms like Montgomery Ward and Sears built their business on mail-order catalogs, which mattered most to
options: (A) wealthy shoppers who lived near big-city department stores and could visit their marble halls in person whenever they wished
(B) customers in small towns and rural areas far from city stores, who could order brand-name goods by mail
(C) factory owners purchasing heavy industrial machinery
(D) recent immigrants arriving at Ellis Island
items.explanation: Mail-order catalogs extended the new consumer culture beyond the cities: customers far from department stores could order advertised, brand-name goods by mail.

option_explanations.A: City shoppers could visit department stores in person; catalogs served those who could not.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Catalogs brought department-store-style goods to small-town and rural customers.
option_explanations.C: Catalogs sold household and consumer goods, not industrial machinery.
option_explanations.D: Newly arrived immigrants were not the catalogs' main market.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — mail-order catalogs (Montgomery Ward, Sears) built the beginnings of a consumer culture

stimulus.image_caption: Electric streetcars on Canal Street, 1907 postcard view.

items.stem: The 1907 view shows electric streetcars on Canal Street. Electric streetcars helped create 'streetcar suburbs' because they
options: (A) allowed families to live farther from their workplaces, separating home from work and making suburban homeownership possible for the middle class
(B) were the first form of public transportation ever used in American cities
(C) carried shoppers to downtown department stores and nowhere else
(D) replaced railroads as the main carriers of freight
items.explanation: Electric streetcars made it practical to commute from farther out, so middle-class families could move to early suburbs — separating the home from the workplace and making homeownership the class's defining aspiration.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Streetcars extended the commuting range, enabling suburbs and middle-class homeownership.
option_explanations.B: Horse-drawn streetcars and omnibuses came before electric ones.
option_explanations.C: Streetcars served commuters across the city, not only shoppers.
option_explanations.D: Streetcars carried passengers within cities; railroads remained the freight carriers.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — electric streetcars let families move to early suburbs (streetcar suburbs), separating home from workplace; homeownership the class's defining aspiration

items.stem: The Gilded Age middle class sent more of its children to high school than any earlier generation and enjoyed more leisure time. Those changes help explain why middle-class Americans became
options: (A) the main source of recruits for factory labor
(B) opponents of every form of government regulation, demanding that business and city life be left entirely free of public control
(C) the audience for the era's reform energy — women's clubs, temperance unions, and the readers of the muckrakers
(D) supporters of a mass return to farm life
items.explanation: More schooling and more leisure gave the middle class the time, literacy, and inclination to fill the era's reform audiences — the clubs, temperance unions, and muckraking magazines.

option_explanations.A: Factory labor drew on immigrants and the working class, not the schooled middle class.
option_explanations.B: The middle class would soon demand regulation — pure food, clean cities, honest government.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Schooling and leisure made the middle class the audience for reform energy.
option_explanations.D: The middle class was moving to streetcar suburbs, not back to farms.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — high schools expanded rapidly; more leisure; audiences for reform energy: women's clubs, temperance unions, readers of the muckrakers

items.stem: The review calls the Gilded Age middle class 'Progressivism's foot soldiers': the clerks and professionals who, in the 1900s, demanded pure food, clean cities, and honest government. This description makes its strongest point about
options: (A) the platform of the Populist Party in the 1890s
(B) the reasons industrial workers joined labor unions to fight for higher wages, shorter hours, and safer conditions in factories and mines
(C) the causes of the Panic of 1893
(D) how a class created by industrialization carried its expectations into the reform politics of the Progressive Era
items.explanation: The point connects the Gilded Age to what followed: the middle class industrialization created became, in the 1900s, the constituency demanding pure food, clean cities, and honest government.

option_explanations.A: Populism was a farmers' movement of the 1890s, not the middle-class reformers of the 1900s.
option_explanations.B: Union members were industrial workers; the 'foot soldiers' described here are clerks and professionals.
option_explanations.C: The Panic of 1893 was an economic depression, unrelated to this claim about reform politics.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The description links the middle class's origins in industrialization to its later reform role.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — this class became Progressivism's foot soldiers: demanded pure food, clean cities, honest government in the 1900s

items.stem: "The middle class was industrialization's most durable political product — it bought the system's promises, then turned around and tried to fix the system's abuses." This claim is best judged as
options: (A) false, because the middle class took no part in reform movements
(B) a reasonable judgment: the middle class embraced the new economy's goods, then supplied many Progressive Era reformers
(C) false, because industrialization created no middle class at all
(D) exaggerated, because only factory workers ever demanded reforms, while the middle class stayed home and ignored public life entirely
items.explanation: The claim fits the evidence: the middle class bought department-store goods and new products, then its clerks and professionals filled the Progressive Era's reform campaigns for pure food, clean cities, and honest government.

option_explanations.A: The middle class filled women's clubs, temperance unions, and the muckrakers' readership.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The claim accurately describes a class that embraced the new economy and then tried to reform it.
option_explanations.C: Industrialization created a large new white-collar middle class.
option_explanations.D: Factory workers organized unions; the reformers described here were middle-class clerks and professionals.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — 'The middle class was industrialization's most durable political product — it bought the system's promises, then turned around and tried to fix the system's abuses.'

items.stem: Unlike the factory workers of the Gilded Age, the new white-collar middle class
options: (A) earned salaries for non-manual work, though their incomes still rose and fell with the economy
(B) owned the corporations that employed them
(C) was untouched by economic depressions
(D) performed manual labor in mills, mines, and factories
items.explanation: White-collar workers lived by salaries rather than wages for manual labor, but those salaries still depended on the economy's ups and downs — they were not owners and not insulated from hard times.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Salaried, non-manual work defined the class, without freeing it from economic cycles.
option_explanations.B: Corporations were owned by investors and shareholders, not by their clerks.
option_explanations.C: Their salaries depended on the economy, so depressions affected them too.
option_explanations.D: Manual labor in mills, mines, and factories was the working class's lot, not the white-collar middle class's.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Gilded Age middle class — white-collar workers whose salaries depended on the economy but whose lives no longer involved manual labor
